'''Natalie M. Batalha''' (born May 14, 1966) is professor of Astronomy and Astrophysics at [[UC Santa Cruz]]. Previously she was a research astronomer in the Space Sciences Division of [[NASA Ames Research Center]] and held the position of Science Team Lead (2010 - 2012), Mission Scientist (2012 - 2016), and Project Scientist (2016 - 2018) on the [[Kepler Mission]], the first mission capable of finding Earth-size planets around other stars.<ref name="NASA-bio"/><ref name="AMES-bio"/><ref name="Kepler-bio"/> Before moving to NASA, Batalha was a Professor of Physics and Astronomy at [[San Jose State University]] (2002 - 2012).

==Biography==
Batalha grew up in the [[San Francisco Bay Area]], and attended the [[University of California, Berkeley]].<ref>{{Cite web|last=Wolchover|first=Natalie|date=2021-12-03|title=The Webb Space Telescope Will Rewrite Cosmic History. If It Works.|url=https://www.quantamagazine.org/why-nasas-james-webb-space-telescope-matters-so-much-20211203/|access-date=2021-12-24|website=Quanta Magazine|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|last1=Ferris|first1=Timothy |last2=Archibald |first2=Timothy|title=Meet Natalie Batalha, the Explorer Who's Searching for Planets Across the Universe|url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/science-nature/natalie-batalha-explorer-searching-planets-across-universe-180967220/|access-date=2021-12-24|website=Smithsonian Magazine|language=en}}</ref> Though she started out as a business major, she switched to physics after learning that everyday occurrences like [[thin-film interference]] (why rainbows appear on soap bubbles and oily puddles) could be described mathematically. During her undergraduate, she worked as a [[Astronomical spectroscopy|stellar spectroscopist]], studying Sun-like stars. After graduating with her bachelor's degree in physics, she pursued a doctorate in astrophysics from [[UC Santa Cruz]], and completed a post-doctoral fellowship in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.<ref name="Kepler-bio"/><ref name="AMES-bio"/>

Batalha is married to Celso Batalha, a Brazilian-born professor of astronomy and physics at a nearby community college, [[Evergreen Valley College]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://sanjosespotlight.com/celso-batalha-gets-low-income-san-jose-students-excited-about-science/|title=Celso Batalha gets low-income San Jose students excited about science|first=Carina|last=Woudenberg|date=June 10, 2000|newspaper=San Jose Spotlight|access-date=2026-04-23}}</ref> Their daughter [[Natasha Batalha]] is also an astronomer. Natalie and Natasha Batalha have collaborated on projects that discover and describe exoplanets found using the [[James Webb Space Telescope]].<ref>{{cite journal | url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-023-00580-6 | doi=10.1038/d41586-023-00580-6 | title=Mother–daughter duo work together to find new worlds | date=2023 | last1=Chen | first1=Sophia | journal=Nature | pmid=36849819 | url-access=subscription }}</ref> 

==Career==

In 1997, [[William Borucki]] added Batalha to the science team and she started work on transit photometry. She has been involved with the Kepler Mission since the design and funding, and as one of the original Co-Investigators was responsible for the selection of the more than 150,000 stars monitored by the telescope. She now works closely with team members at Ames Research Center to identify viable planets from the data of the Kepler mission. She led the analysis that yielded the discovery in 2011 of [[Kepler 10b]], the first confirmed rocky planet outside the [[Solar System]].<ref name="Kepler-bio"/><ref name="Lemonick-2012"/>

In November 2017, the [[Space Telescope Science Institute]] selected 13 programs for Director's Discretionary Early Release Science (DD-ERS) on the [[James Webb Space Telescope]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Selections Made for the JWST Director's Discretionary Early Release Science Program |url=https://jwst.stsci.edu/news-events/news/News%2520items/selections-made-for-the-jwst-directors-discretionary-early-release-science-program |archive-url=https://wayback.archive-it.org/all/20180808190059/https://jwst.stsci.edu/news-events/news/News%2520items/selections-made-for-the-jwst-directors-discretionary-early-release-science-program |url-status=dead |archive-date=2018-08-08 |access-date=2022-05-30 |website=wayback.archive-it.org}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=DD-ERS |url=http://www.stsci.edu/home/jwst/science-execution/approved-programs/dd-ers |access-date=2022-05-30 |website=STScI.edu |language=en}}</ref> Of a total of 460 observation hours allocated, Batalha's project, 'The Transiting Exoplanet Community Early Release Science Program', was awarded 86.9 hours; the highest of any DD-ERS program on the JWST.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Batalha |first1=Natalie |last2=Bean |first2=Jacob |last3=Stevenson |first3=Kevin |title=The Transiting Exoplanet Community Early Release Science Program (Natalie Batalha) |url=https://www.stsci.edu/files/live/sites/www/files/home/jwst/news-events/news/pre-2018/_documents/ers-1366-batalha.pdf }}</ref> These observation hours are allocated to be used during the first five months of the telescope's operation.

Batalha leads the UC Santa Cruz Astrobiology Initiative, a collaborative, interdisciplinary initiative dedicated to the study of the origin, evolution, and distribution of life in the universe.

Following the successful launch of the [[James Webb Space Telescope]] in 2021, Batalha and a team of researchers found unambiguous evidence of [[carbon dioxide]] in the atmosphere of an exoplanet.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=The JWST Transiting Exoplanet Community Early Release Science Team |last2=Ahrer |first2=Eva-Maria |last3=Alderson |first3=Lili |last4=Batalha |first4=Natalie M. |last5=Batalha |first5=Natasha E. |last6=Bean |first6=Jacob L. |last7=Beatty |first7=Thomas G. |last8=Bell |first8=Taylor J. |last9=Benneke |first9=Björn |last10=Berta-Thompson |first10=Zachory K. |last11=Carter |first11=Aarynn L. |last12=Crossfield |first12=Ian J. M. |last13=Espinoza |first13=Néstor |last14=Feinstein |first14=Adina D. |last15=Fortney |first15=Jonathan J. |date=2023-02-23 |title=Identification of carbon dioxide in an exoplanet atmosphere |journal=Nature |volume=614 |issue=7949 |pages=649–652 |doi=10.1038/s41586-022-05269-w |pmid=36055338 |pmc=9946830 |arxiv=2208.11692 |bibcode=2023Natur.614..649J |issn=0028-0836|doi-access=free }}</ref> The team used JWST to observe a Saturn-mass planet called [[WASP-39b]] which orbits very close to a Sun-like star about 700 light-years from Earth.

Batalha, along with Mark Clampin, Astrophysics Division Director, National Aeronautics and Space Administration, and Steven L. Finkelstein, Professor of Astronomy, University of Texas at Austin, testified before the House of Representatives Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, Subcommittee on Space and Aeronautics in 2022.<ref>{{Citation |title=House Science, Space, and Technology Hearing on Initial Results from the James Webb Space Telescope | date=17 November 2022 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4rqxCrVtqdE |access-date=2023-10-02 |language=en}}</ref>

Batalha and the JWST Transiting Exoplanet Early Release Science Team used the James Webb Space Telescope in 2023 to identify water vapor in the atmosphere of WASP-18b and make a temperature map of the planet as it slipped behind, and reappeared from, its star.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Coulombe |first1=Louis-Philippe |last2=Benneke |first2=Björn |last3=Challener |first3=Ryan |last4=Piette |first4=Anjali A. A. |last5=Wiser |first5=Lindsey S. |last6=Mansfield |first6=Megan |last7=MacDonald |first7=Ryan J. |last8=Beltz |first8=Hayley |last9=Feinstein |first9=Adina D. |last10=Radica |first10=Michael |last11=Savel |first11=Arjun B. |last12=Dos Santos |first12=Leonardo A. |last13=Bean |first13=Jacob L. |last14=Parmentier |first14=Vivien |last15=Wong |first15=Ian |date=August 2023 |title=A broadband thermal emission spectrum of the ultra-hot Jupiter WASP-18b |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=620 |issue=7973 |pages=292–298 |doi=10.1038/s41586-023-06230-1 |pmid=37257843 |pmc=10412449 |arxiv=2301.08192 |bibcode=2023Natur.620..292C |issn=1476-4687|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Presentations==
Batalha presented 'A Planet for Goldilocks' at [[Talks at Google]] in 2016. She presented 'From Lava Worlds to Living Worlds' at [[Breakthrough Initiatives]] in 2019.<ref name="Goldilocks"/><ref name="Living-Worlds"/>

==Recognition==
In 2011, Batalha was awarded NASA's [[NASA Exceptional Public Service Medal|Exceptional Public Service Medal]] for outstanding leadership of the Kepler Science Team. 

In 2017, Batalha and two other exoplanet scientists were named to Time Magazine's 100 Most Influential People in the World.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://time.com/collection/2017-time-100/4742707/natalie-batalha-guillem-anglada-escude-michael-gillon/ | title=Natalie Batalha, Guillem Anglada-EscudÃ© and MichaÃ«l Gillon: The Worldâ€™s 100 Most Influential People }}</ref>
In the same year, Batalha won Smithsonian Magazine's American Ingenuity Award in Physical Sciences.<ref name="Ingenuity Awards">{{cite web |title=2017 American Ingenuity Award Winners |url=https://www.smithsonianmag.com/ingenuity/2017-winners/ |website=Smithsonian Magazine |publisher=Smithsonian |accessdate=11 October 2018 |archive-date=27 December 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191227010236/https://www.smithsonianmag.com/ingenuity/2017-winners/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> 

In 2018, Batalha received the UC Santa Cruz Alumni Achievement award.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://news.ucsc.edu/2018/10/batalha-alumni-award.html | title=Astronomer Natalie Batalha to receive Alumni Achievement Award }}</ref>  

In 2019, Batalha earned an honorary doctorate from the Faculty of Science and Technology at the [[Uppsala University|University of Uppsala]], Sweden.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.uu.se/en/about-uu/academic-traditions/traditions/honorary-doctorates/honorary-doctors-of-the-faculty-of-science-and-technology | title=Honorary Doctors of the Faculty of Science and Technology - Uppsala University | date=8 June 2023 }}</ref>

Batalha was elected a member of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2019<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.amacad.org/news/2019-members-announcement|title=New 2019 Academy Members Announced|publisher=[[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]|date=April 17, 2019}}</ref> and a Legacy Fellow of the [[American Astronomical Society]] in 2020.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://aas.org/grants-and-prizes/aas-fellows|title=AAS Fellows|publisher=AAS|accessdate=27 September 2020}}</ref> 

In 2020, Batalha was appointed as a UC Presidential Chair for her work on the UCSC Astrobiology Initiative.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://science.ucsc.edu/natalie-batalha-is-appointed-the-ucsc-presidential-chair/ | title=Natalie Batalha is appointed the UCSC Presidential Chair | date=23 June 2021 }}</ref>

Batalha has been awarded several named lectureships, including the James T. Bunyan Lecturer (2011, Stanford University), the Rittenhouse Lecturer (2015, University of Pennsylvania), the Walter Stibbs Lecturer (2016, University of Sydney), the Beatrice Hill Tinsley Lecturer (2017, New Zealand), the Carl Sagan Distinguished Lecturer (2018, Cornell University), the Celsius Lecturer, (2018, Uppsala University), the John N. Bahcall Distinguished Lecturer (2019, Space Telescope Science Institute), and the UCSC Faculty Research Lecturer (2024, University of California, Santa Cruz).
